title: How do you know this system is broken before your users tell you?
summary: Tests whether you can name the specific signals and thresholds that catch a problem early — not just answer "we'd have monitoring."

slides.markdown:
"We'd have monitoring" is not an answer — every candidate says that. The interviewer is testing whether you can name the *specific* signals and thresholds that catch a real problem before it becomes a support ticket flood.

This question shows up as a follow-up to almost any HLD design: once you've drawn the boxes and arrows, the interviewer wants to know how you'd find out, in production, that one of those boxes quietly stopped working. The strong answer names concrete signals (latency percentiles, error rate, saturation) and ties each one to a specific alert threshold, not a vague promise to "watch dashboards."

Two questions are worth asking out loud before you dive in. First: is this about full outages, or gradual degradation too? A health check catches "the process crashed"; it says nothing about "the process is up but every request now takes 3 seconds."

Second: what's the cost of detecting a problem 5 minutes late versus 5 seconds late, for *this specific* system? A batch analytics pipeline can tolerate minutes of detection lag; a payment-authorization path cannot. That cost is what should set your alert thresholds and your on-call urgency — asking it signals you're designing detection to the system's actual stakes, not applying a generic template.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: the golden signals
slides.markdown:
Anchor your answer on the four **golden signals**: **latency** (how long requests take, especially at the p99, where the worst experiences hide), **traffic** (requests per second, so you can tell a real anomaly from a normal diurnal dip), **errors** (the rate of failed requests), and **saturation** (how full your resources are — CPU, memory, connection pools, queues).

The discipline is alerting on the signals that predict or reflect *user* pain, not just server health. A server can report "I'm up" while every real request queues behind an exhausted connection pool — that's exactly the gap the golden signals are built to close. For how to turn these signals into a formal target, see [metrics and SLIs/SLOs](metrics-and-slis-slos).

Make it concrete with numbers. You'd alert on **p99 latency crossing 500ms** for a service whose normal p99 sits around 150ms — a threshold picked from the actual baseline, not a round number pulled from nowhere. And you'd alert on a **5xx error-rate burn rate** — the rate at which a service is consuming its error budget — rather than a single static "errors > 0" trigger that fires on every routine blip.

Both thresholds should trace back to something a user would notice: 500ms is where checkout starts to feel sluggish; a fast error-budget burn means you're on track to blow your monthly SLO within hours, not months.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the health check that lies
slides.markdown:
Walk through a scenario where health-check-only monitoring fails outright. A checkout service's CPU and memory both look completely normal — health checks return 200 OK all day. But its p99 latency has crept from 200ms to 3 seconds because the database connection pool is exhausted: every request now waits in a queue for a connection before it can even start real work.

A health-check-only dashboard shows all-green the entire time. Every real user is stuck on a spinner. This is the concrete case for why "the process responds" and "the system works" are different claims, and why latency and saturation signals catch what a bare liveness probe cannot.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: saturation as the leading indicator
slides.markdown:
![Saturation signals rising minutes before p99 latency spikes](assets/saturation-leads-latency.svg)

Saturation metrics are your lead time. Connection-pool usage at 95%, a queue depth that's been climbing for ten minutes, a disk approaching full — none of these are user-facing failures yet, but each predicts one.

Alerting on saturation lets you act *before* latency or error rate move at all — restart a leaking pool, add capacity, or clear a queue while it's still an internal metric, not an incident.

assets.alt: Saturation signals rising minutes before p99 latency spikes

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
More signals catch more failure modes, but every signal you alert on is one more thing a human has to triage during an incident — and one more thing that can page someone at 2am for nothing.

| Signal set | Catches | Triage cost |
|---|---|---|
| Golden signals only (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) | Most user-facing failures | Low — a handful of dashboards, easy to reason about |
| + infrastructure-internal metrics (GC pauses, thread pools, disk IOPS) | Deeper root causes, faster diagnosis once paged | Higher — more noise, more false positives to tune out |

Start from the four golden signals, since they map directly to user pain. Add infrastructure-internal signals selectively, once you know which ones this system's real incidents actually hinge on.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: your error rate is normal but users are still complaining
slides.markdown:
This follow-up is testing whether your detection stops at the server's front door. The answer: something client-side is failing that your server-side metrics never see, or averaging away.

Two concrete candidates. **Real user monitoring (RUM)** or JS error rates catch failures that never reach your backend at all — a broken client-side redirect, a JS exception before the request fires. **Mobile crash rates** catch a client crashing on a response your server considers a perfectly successful 200. The other candidate: a partial-degradation signal your server-side average smooths over — one shard or one region failing while the aggregate error rate across all traffic still looks fine.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: catching a slow, gradual degradation
slides.markdown:
A static threshold ('alert if p99 > 500ms') never fires on a creep from 150ms to 480ms — it stays technically under the line the whole way, even as the trend is clearly worsening.

The fix is **trend-based alerting**: compare this week's p99 against last week's same-day-same-hour baseline, or run anomaly detection that flags a metric drifting away from its historical pattern, even while every single point stays under a static threshold. This catches the class of failure a single-jump alarm is structurally blind to — a slow resource leak, a creeping index bloat, a cache hit rate eroding gradually as data grows past what it was sized for.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: uptime pings and nothing else
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have monitoring — a health check pings the service every 30 seconds and pages us if it stops responding."

**Why it's wrong:** a health check answers one narrow question — is the process alive and accepting connections — and says nothing about whether requests flowing through it are slow, erroring for a subset of users, or stuck behind a saturated dependency. The checkout-service scenario earlier in this topic is the canonical failure of this exact setup: every health check green, every real user stuck.

**Correct model:** treat liveness as the *minimum* bar, not the detection strategy. Layer the golden signals on top — latency percentiles, error rate, saturation — so a technically-alive-but-actually-broken system still pages someone.

Detection means alerting on the golden signals — latency (especially p99), traffic, errors, and saturation — with thresholds tied to actual user pain, not server-health trivia like "is the process up."

Saturation metrics (connection-pool usage, queue depth) are your earliest warning, often minutes ahead of latency or errors moving at all. Layer in client-side signals (RUM, crash rates) to catch failures your backend never sees, and trend-based alerting to catch a slow creep a static threshold would miss entirely. The pitfall to avoid out loud: a health check alone is necessary, never sufficient.
